books.section: Topic 6.6 The Rise of Industrial Capitalism
America Transformed into the Industrial Giant of the World (1870–1910)
Industrialization, Corporate Consolidation, and the Gospel of Wealth

primary_sources: Andrew Carnegie, “Wealth” (The Gospel of Wealth), North American Review, June 1889

stimulus.text: The problem of our age is the proper administration of wealth, so that the ties of brotherhood may still bind together the rich and poor in harmonious relationship. The conditions of human life have not only been changed, but revolutionized, within the past few hundred years. In former days there was little difference between the dwelling, dress, food, and environment of the chief and those of his retainers. … The contrast between the palace of the millionaire and the cottage of the laborer with us to-day measures the change which has come with civilization. But whether the change be for good or ill, it is upon us, beyond our power to alter, and, therefore, to be accepted and made the best of.
stimulus.source_note: Andrew Carnegie, “Wealth,” North American Review 148 (June 1889). Public domain; wording and punctuation follow the original North American Review text. Ellipsis marks an omission between complete sentences.

stem: Carnegie’s contrast between “the palace of the millionaire and the cottage of the laborer” is meant to show

options.text: that rich and poor lived alike in the past
options.misconception: Carnegie says the chief and his retainers lived alike in former days, but the contrast measures how far apart rich and poor now stand.

options.text: that wealth should be divided equally by the government
options.misconception: Carnegie never calls for the government to divide wealth equally.

options.text: how greatly inequality had grown with civilization
that the laborer owned the palace
options.misconception: Carnegie gives the palace to the millionaire and the cottage to the laborer.

rationales.A: The past likeness is the starting point; the contrast shows how much has changed since.
rationales.B: Carnegie wants rich men to give wealth away themselves, not the government to divide it.
rationales.C: The palace and the cottage measure the change civilization has brought.
rationales.D: Carnegie puts the millionaire in the palace and the laborer in the cottage.
rationales.general:
Ask what the contrast measures.
1. In former days, Carnegie says, chief and retainers lived much alike.
2. Now the millionaire lives in a palace and the laborer in a cottage.
3. The gap between the two measures the change civilization has brought.
4. Background from the books: industrialization made a few men very rich while most workers stayed poor.
Remember: a contrast between two pictures measures the distance between them.
